The distinction between 'not tracked because ignored' and 'removed from history' is a genuine security and hygiene issue practitioners routinely get wrong: adding a pattern to `.gitignore` after a secret has already been committed does nothing to remove that secret from the repository's history, and the only real remedies are rewriting history (`git filter-repo` or the older `BFG Repo-Cleaner`, both of which rewrite every commit hash downstream and require force-pushing and coordinating with every collaborator) or, more reliably, simply treating the leaked secret as compromised and rotating it, since history rewriting on a shared repository is disruptive and easy to do incorrectly. `.gitignore` pattern precedence has real edge cases: a more specific pattern later in the file can override an earlier, broader one, and a negation pattern (`!important.log`) cannot re-include a file inside a directory that was ignored with a trailing slash, a frequently-hit gotcha when someone tries to selectively un-ignore a single file inside an otherwise-ignored folder. Teams commonly maintain a `.gitignore` template (language- or framework-specific starting points, like those GitHub provides) and layer project-specific patterns on top, since manually enumerating every build artifact, cache folder, and editor temp file a modern toolchain generates by hand is both tedious and easy to get incompletely right on the first try. Secret scanning tools that run in CI or as a pre-commit hook, scanning every diff for key-shaped strings regardless of `.gitignore` contents, exist specifically because `.gitignore` alone is a preventive convention that relies on someone remembering to add the right pattern before the first commit, not an enforced guarantee.

At Apple's scale, secret and sensitive-data exclusion from source control is enforced by automated pre-commit and CI-level scanning that blocks a push containing a credential-shaped string, treating `.gitignore` as a helpful first line of defense rather than the actual security boundary, precisely because a `.gitignore` entry is a convention any individual commit can bypass with `git add -f`, deliberately or by mistake. Large-scale monorepos generate `.gitignore` patterns programmatically or enforce them centrally, since manually maintaining a consistent ignore file across thousands of contributors and constantly-changing build tooling does not scale, and an inconsistent `.gitignore` across a large codebase is itself a recurring source of accidentally-committed build artifacts bloating repository size over time. An open, still partly unsolved engineering problem industry-wide is fully preventing secret leakage into version control while keeping developer workflow friction low, since every layer of defense, `.gitignore`, pre-commit hooks, CI scanning, has gaps or can be bypassed under enough time pressure, which is why serious organizations treat 'assume any leaked secret is compromised the moment it is committed, regardless of how quickly it is removed' as the operating assumption rather than relying on any single preventive layer holding perfectly.

read-csv.def: pandas functions for loading and saving tables: `read_csv` reads plain text; `to_parquet`/`read_parquet` use a faster, smaller binary format.
levels: `read_csv` is like unpacking a box of index cards written in plain handwriting into a neat table you can use. `to_parquet` is like repacking that same table into a special, compact suitcase that is much faster to open again later. `read_parquet` is opening that suitcase back up, quick as a flash.

`read_csv` is a pandas function that loads a comma-separated text file into a table (a DataFrame) you can work with in Python. `to_parquet` saves a DataFrame in Parquet format instead, a compact binary file type that is much smaller and faster to read back than plain text CSV. `read_parquet` loads a Parquet file back into a DataFrame. This course typically loads raw PeMS data with `read_csv` once, since that is the format it arrives in, and then saves processed versions with `to_parquet` so later steps load much faster.

`pd.read_csv('file.csv', parse_dates=['timestamp'])` reads a comma-separated file into a DataFrame and, with the `parse_dates` argument, converts specified columns straight into proper datetime objects as it reads, rather than leaving them as plain text. `df.to_parquet('file.parquet')` writes the same DataFrame to Parquet, a columnar binary format (through the pyarrow library) that stores each column's data type explicitly and compresses it, typically making the file several times smaller than the equivalent CSV and much faster to read back with `pd.read_parquet('file.parquet')`. `pd.read_csv(file, chunksize=100_000)` reads a huge CSV in chunks of 100,000 rows at a time instead of loading the whole thing into memory at once, which matters for a file too large to fit in RAM. Because CSV stores everything as plain text, every value must be re-parsed (a number turned back from digits into an actual number) every single time the file is read, which Parquet avoids by storing typed, already-structured data.

CSV is a row-oriented, text-based format with no enforced schema: every value is a string until something (like `parse_dates`, or pandas's own type inference) interprets it, which makes CSV files simple and universally readable but fragile, since a column pandas infers as integers in one file might be read as floats or strings in another if a single row has a missing or malformed value, silently changing downstream behavior. Parquet is column-oriented and self-describing: it stores an explicit schema (column names and types) inside the file itself, compresses each column separately using an algorithm suited to that column's data (which works especially well on repetitive data like categorical station IDs), and lets a reader load only specific columns without reading the whole file, called column pruning, none of which CSV supports. `chunksize` in `read_csv` returns an iterator of DataFrames rather than one big DataFrame, letting a pipeline process an arbitrarily large file in bounded memory by processing and discarding each chunk before loading the next; the equivalent capability in Parquet, reading only certain row groups, is often faster still because Parquet's metadata lets a reader skip irrelevant sections without scanning them at all. Round-tripping data through CSV and back can silently lose information, like a leading zero in a station ID being reinterpreted as an integer and dropped, whereas round-tripping through Parquet preserves the exact schema and values because the types are stored explicitly rather than re-inferred each time.

The performance gap between CSV and Parquet compounds directly with data scale: for a ten-million-row PeMS panel, `read_csv` must tokenize and parse every field as text on every load, an O(n) cost with a large constant factor, while `read_parquet` can skip type inference entirely and, for column-selective queries, skip reading unneeded columns from disk altogether, which is why a serious pipeline reads raw CSV exactly once, converts it to Parquet, and does every subsequent load from the Parquet copy. Parquet's per-column compression and encoding (dictionary encoding for low-cardinality columns like `station_id` or `direction`, run-length encoding for repeated values) means the same logical data can occupy dramatically less disk space than CSV, and disk I/O, not CPU, is frequently the actual bottleneck for large tabular pipelines, so this space savings translates directly into faster load times, not just smaller files. A subtlety practitioners often miss is that `parse_dates` in `read_csv` uses a general-purpose date parser that can silently misinterpret ambiguous date formats (is `01/02/2023` January 2nd or February 1st) unless an explicit `date_format` is supplied, whereas Parquet, once written with a specific datetime dtype, has no such ambiguity on read since the type itself, not a re-parsed string, is what is stored. Schema evolution, adding a new column to a dataset that already has years of Parquet files written in an older schema, requires deliberate handling (a schema-merging read, or a migration step), since naively concatenating Parquet files with mismatched schemas can either fail outright or silently produce nulls in ways a CSV-based pipeline, with its total absence of enforced schema, would not even flag as an issue worth handling.

In production data engineering, Parquet (or a closely related columnar format like ORC) is the standard storage format for any dataset at meaningful scale, precisely because its column pruning and predicate pushdown (skipping row groups that cannot match a filter, based on stored min/max statistics per column) let query engines read a small fraction of a huge dataset's bytes to answer a narrow query, something CSV's row-oriented, unindexed structure cannot support at all. Apple-scale data pipelines that do still ingest CSV (from an external partner, a legacy system, or a one-off export) typically treat that CSV ingestion as a single, tightly-controlled boundary step, validating and converting to a typed columnar format immediately, rather than letting CSV's untyped, unvalidated nature propagate deeper into a system where a subtle parsing ambiguity could silently corrupt data used across many downstream consumers. An open, still-evolving area is table formats built on top of Parquet, like Apache Iceberg and Delta Lake, that add transactional guarantees, schema evolution, and time-travel querying that raw Parquet files alone do not provide, addressing exactly the schema-evolution and consistency gaps that become a real operational problem once a dataset is written to and read by many different jobs over a long period of time.

pathlib.def: Python's standard-library module for working with file and folder paths as objects instead of raw strings.
levels: pathlib is a helper that lets you treat a file's address, like where a toy is stored on a shelf, as its own kind of object instead of just a plain sentence of words. Instead of gluing pieces of text together to build an address, you can just say 'go into this shelf, then that box' step by step. It also knows how to check whether a file is really there.

pathlib is a standard Python module for handling file and folder paths as objects, instead of as plain strings glued together. `Path('data') / 'pems' / 'file.csv'` builds a path piece by piece using the `/` operator, which automatically uses the right slash for whatever operating system the code runs on. A `Path` object has useful built-in checks, like `.exists()` to see if a file is really there, and `.mkdir()` to create a folder. This is safer than manually building paths with string concatenation, which can easily produce a wrong path, especially across different operating systems.

`from pathlib import Path` and `Path('data/pems') / 'station_meta.csv'` builds a path object that represents that location without necessarily creating anything on disk yet; the `/` operator is overloaded specifically to join path segments, correctly using backslashes on Windows and forward slashes on macOS or Linux without the code needing to know which. Common methods include `.exists()` (does this path point to something real), `.is_file()` and `.is_dir()`, `.mkdir(parents=True, exist_ok=True)` (create a folder and any missing parent folders, without erroring if it already exists), `.glob('*.csv')` (list every file matching a pattern), and `.stem` / `.suffix` (a filename without its extension, and just its extension). `Path(__file__).parent` gives the folder containing the currently-running script, a common way to build paths relative to the code itself rather than relative to wherever the terminal happens to be when the script runs.

Representing a path as a structured object rather than a raw string is a deliberate API design that prevents an entire class of bugs: string-based path code that manually concatenates with `+` or a hardcoded `/` breaks on Windows (which uses `\`), mishandles trailing slashes, and offers no built-in validation, whereas `pathlib`'s `Path` objects encapsulate platform-specific behavior behind a single, consistent interface and expose filesystem operations (existence checks, globbing, creating directories) as methods rather than requiring separate calls into the `os` or `os.path` modules. `pathlib` distinguishes between a path that merely represents a location (usable even for a location that does not exist, like a path you are about to create) and an actual filesystem query (`.exists()`, `.stat()`), which matters because path objects are cheap and side-effect-free to construct, while the query methods actually touch the filesystem and can be slow or fail if permissions are wrong. Relative paths resolved against the current working directory are a common source of bugs in scripts invoked from different locations (cron, a different terminal session, a CI runner), which is why `Path(__file__).parent`, resolving relative to the script's own location rather than wherever it happens to be launched from, is standard practice in production-quality code. `pathlib`'s `Path` objects implement the `os.PathLike` protocol, so they can be passed directly to most standard library and third-party functions (like `open()` or `pd.read_csv()`) that expect a path, without needing to convert to a string first, which is part of why the module has largely replaced manual `os.path` string manipulation in modern Python code.

`pathlib`'s object-oriented design also enables method chaining and composability that string-based path manipulation does not naturally support, like `sorted(Path('data').glob('**/*.csv'))` recursively finding and sorting every CSV file under a directory tree in one expression, which would require several lines of manual string handling and `os.walk` logic using the older `os.path` approach. A subtlety that trips up newcomers is that `Path.glob()` returns a generator, not a list, so it is consumed once; iterating it a second time without re-calling `.glob()` silently yields nothing, which looks like a bug in the code being iterated rather than in how the generator itself was used. Cross-platform path handling has real edge cases beyond just the slash direction: case sensitivity differs (Linux filesystems are typically case-sensitive, macOS and Windows typically are not by default), and path length limits differ (historically much shorter on Windows), so code tested only on one platform can fail in subtle, hard-to-reproduce ways on another, which `pathlib` reduces but does not fully eliminate as a source of bugs. `Path.resolve()` converts a relative or symlink-containing path into its canonical absolute form, which matters for correctly comparing two paths that might refer to the same file through different relative routes, a comparison that naive string equality on unresolved paths would get wrong.

In production data and ML pipelines operating across heterogeneous environments (a developer's Mac, a Linux CI runner, a cloud batch job), consistent path handling via `pathlib` is one small but real contributor to reproducibility, since a pipeline that silently depends on a particular OS's path separator or working-directory assumption is a common, avoidable source of 'works on my machine' failures when a job moves from a laptop to a scheduled production environment. Larger data engineering systems increasingly work with paths that are not local filesystem paths at all, like `s3://bucket/key` or other cloud object-store URIs, and libraries built to feel like `pathlib` (such as `cloudpathlib` or fsspec-based path objects) extend the same object-oriented, operator-overloaded interface to remote storage, letting pipeline code written against a `pathlib`-like interface run largely unchanged whether data lives on local disk or in cloud storage. An open practical challenge industry-wide is unifying local and remote path handling cleanly enough that pipeline code does not need to branch on where its data actually lives, since local filesystem semantics (atomic renames, direct random-access reads and writes) do not map perfectly onto object-store semantics (eventually-consistent listings, no true atomic rename), and `pathlib`-style abstractions can paper over, but not fully eliminate, those underlying differences.

init.def: The method that runs automatically when a class creates a new object, setting up its starting attributes.
levels: `__init__` is the special job a class does the very first moment a new copy of it is born, kind of like a nurse writing your name and birthday on a bracelet the moment you arrive. You do not have to call it yourself; it just happens automatically whenever you make something new from a class. Whatever gets written down in that first moment sticks with that one particular copy from then on.

`__init__` is a special method inside a Python class that runs automatically every time you create a new object from that class, and it is where you set up the object's starting attributes (its stored values). `class Station: def __init__(self, station_id, freeway): self.station_id = station_id; self.freeway = freeway` defines a class where creating `Station('400017', 'I-880')` automatically stores those two values on the new object. A class is a blueprint for creating objects, and `__init__` is the part of that blueprint that fills in each new object's specific details. Every method inside a class, including `__init__`, takes `self` as its first argument, which refers to the specific object being worked with.

`__init__(self, ...)` is called automatically right after Python creates a new, empty instance of a class, and its job is to attach whatever starting attributes the object needs by assigning to `self.attribute_name`; unlike some other languages, `__init__` does not itself allocate the object (a separate, rarely-overridden method called `__new__` does that), it only initializes an already-created one. A class like `class Registry: def __init__(self, meta_path): self.df = pd.read_csv(meta_path); self.neighbors_cache = {}` uses `__init__` to load data and set up internal state the moment a `Registry` object is constructed, so every method on that object, like `neighbors(station_id)`, can rely on `self.df` already being populated. Default argument values in `__init__`, like `def __init__(self, cache_size=100)`, let an object be created with sensible defaults while still allowing customization, `Registry(meta_path, cache_size=500)`, without every caller needing to specify every parameter. `__init__` should generally avoid doing anything that can silently fail or take a long time without clear feedback, since a failure inside `__init__` prevents the object from ever being successfully created at all.

`__init__` is one of Python's dunder ('double underscore') methods, a family of specially-named methods the language calls automatically at defined points, and understanding `__init__` as part of that broader protocol (alongside `__repr__` for how an object prints, `__eq__` for how it compares equal, `__len__` for what `len()` returns) clarifies that object construction in Python is itself just one hook in a larger, consistent, overridable object model rather than a special case. A very common and consequential bug is using a mutable default argument in `__init__`, like `def __init__(self, tags=[])`, because default argument values are evaluated exactly once when the function is defined, not once per call, so every object created without an explicit `tags` argument ends up silently sharing and mutating the very same list object; the correct pattern is `def __init__(self, tags=None): self.tags = tags if tags is not None else []`. Inheritance interacts with `__init__` in a way that requires explicit handling: a subclass that defines its own `__init__` does not automatically also run the parent class's `__init__` unless it explicitly calls `super().__init__(...)`, so forgetting that call silently skips whatever setup the parent class's constructor was responsible for. Type hints and dataclasses (`@dataclass`) can auto-generate a correct `__init__` from a class's declared fields, which reduces the amount of hand-written, easy-to-get-subtly-wrong constructor boilerplate for classes whose main job is just holding a fixed set of named attributes.

The mutable-default-argument trap is a direct consequence of Python's function objects being created once, at definition time, and their default argument values living as part of that single function object's state for its entire lifetime, which is a broader lesson about Python's object model, not a quirk specific to `__init__`; the same bug can bite any function with a mutable default, and recognizing the pattern (a default value that is a list, dict, or set) is a genuinely useful, transferable debugging skill. `__init__` versus `__new__` matters concretely for immutable types and certain design patterns: because tuples, strings and other immutable built-ins must have their entire value fixed at creation, subclassing them correctly sometimes requires overriding `__new__`, not `__init__`, since by the time `__init__` runs, the immutable object's value is already fixed and cannot be modified further, a subtlety that surprises even experienced Python programmers who have only ever needed to override `__init__`. Class attributes (declared directly in the class body, outside `__init__`) versus instance attributes (assigned inside `__init__` via `self.`) are frequently confused, and this confusion combines badly with the mutable-default problem: a mutable class attribute is shared across every instance of the class exactly the same way a mutable default argument is, for the same underlying reason, an easy trap for anyone who has not internalized the distinction between class-level and instance-level state. Complex `__init__` methods that do significant work (loading files, opening network connections, expensive computation) make objects harder to test in isolation and harder to construct cheaply for things like unit tests, which is why a common design discipline is keeping `__init__` limited to simple attribute assignment and moving expensive setup into a separate method or a factory function called explicitly when that work is actually needed.

In production codebases at scale, constructor design (what `__init__` does, and what it deliberately defers) is a real architectural decision: dependency injection patterns pass already-constructed dependencies into `__init__` rather than having the constructor build them internally, specifically so objects remain easy to test with mock or fake dependencies and so a single, centrally-configured object graph, not scattered `__init__` calls, controls how a whole system's components are wired together. Frameworks and libraries used at scale (like dataclasses, attrs, or pydantic models) exist substantially to eliminate hand-written `__init__` boilerplate and its associated bug surface (the mutable-default trap chief among them) by auto-generating a correct constructor from declared, typed fields, which both reduces bugs and makes an object's expected shape self-documenting from its class definition alone. An open, still-debated design question across the Python ecosystem is how much validation and complexity belongs directly inside `__init__` (fail fast, the moment an invalid object would be created) versus deferred to a separate validation step or factory function, since eager validation in the constructor catches errors early but can make objects more expensive or awkward to construct in contexts, like deserializing untrusted data or building test fixtures, where a temporarily invalid intermediate state is sometimes genuinely necessary.
